Rare events carry more information than common ones. This lesson quantifies
that statement.

## Information and probability

A report of a near-certain event eliminates no uncertainty; a report of an
improbable event eliminates a great deal. Information content is a property
of the event's probability.

<Figure src="./figures/rarity.svg" alt="Probability versus information carried" caption="Low probability, high information." />

<Definition title="surprisal">
The surprisal of an event $x$ with probability $p(x)$ is
$I(x) = -\log_2 p(x)$, measured in bits.
</Definition>

<Example>
A fair coin lands heads: $I = -\log_2 \tfrac{1}{2} = 1$ bit.
</Example>

## Exercises

<Exercise>
Compute the surprisal, in bits, of a fair coin landing heads.

<Solution>
$-\log_2(1/2) = 1$ bit.
</Solution>
</Exercise>

<References>
1. C. E. Shannon, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," 1948.
</References>
